summary: Defines three channel binding types for TLS, named tls-unique, tls-server-end-point and tls-unique-for-telnet, following RFC 5056. Based on implementation experience, it changes the original definition of tls-unique in the IANA registry. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Channel binding lets an application connect its sign-in process to the particular TLS connection it uses. This RFC defines three ways to create that connection-specific information and warns that the revised tls-unique definition differs from its earlier registration.

questions: what is channel binding in tls
subtitle: Three ways for an application to bind authentication to the TLS connection carrying it.

tldr.problem: Applications that authenticate over TLS need a way to show that the authentication belongs to the same protected connection. Three TLS channel-binding types had been registered, but their definitions needed clarification and one did not match implementation experience.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines channel-binding data from a TLS Finished message, a hash of the server certificate, or Finished messages arranged for TELNET. It also recommends which types applications should use and requires TLS APIs to expose the needed data.
tldr.outcome: It re-registers the three types and changes tls-unique in a backwards-incompatible way. The unit metadata says RFC 5929 is updated by RFC 9266.

today: RFC 5929 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9266. It defines three channel-binding types and changes the registration for tls-unique.

sections.title: Why TLS Channel Bindings Are Defined
sections.content:
A channel binding gives an application data that identifies the secure channel carrying its communication. RFC 5929 defines three TLS channel-binding types and updates their existing IANA registrations to match implementations.

The RFC highlights a compatibility change: the revised definition of tls-unique differs from the original registry definition. Applications using this type need to account for the new behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can use channel-binding data to check that a sign-in belongs to the TLS connection it is using. This RFC defines three sources for that data and changes the earlier meaning of tls-unique.

sections.title: The tls-unique Binding Data
sections.content:
tls-unique is the first TLS Finished message sent in the most recent handshake of the connection. A Finished message is a TLS handshake value that both endpoints can use as channel-binding data. The definition applies to a connection, not a reusable session.

If the connection is renegotiated, the latest handshake supplies the value. The binding can therefore change during authentication and cause an otherwise valid attempt to fail. Servers MUST NOT request renegotiation during application authentication, and clients SHOULD NOT start it during that process.
sections.plainLanguage: For tls-unique, both sides use the first Finished value from the latest TLS handshake. Because renegotiation can change that value, applications should avoid renegotiating while a sign-in is underway.

sections.title: The Server-Certificate Binding
sections.content:
tls-server-end-point is a hash of the server certificate as it appears in the TLS Certificate message. The hash algorithm follows the certificate signature algorithm: use SHA-256 when that algorithm uses MD5 or SHA-1, and otherwise use its single hash function.

If the signature algorithm uses no hash or several hash functions, the RFC leaves this binding undefined. This type is available only when the TLS cipher suite uses a server certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: This type uses a hash, or short fingerprint, of the server certificate. It is available only when the TLS connection includes a server certificate, and some certificate algorithms leave the fingerprint undefined.

sections.title: The TELNET-Specific Binding
sections.content:
tls-unique-for-telnet supports a proposed TELNET StartTLS extension and its authentication mechanisms. The client combines its and the server's Finished values in client-then-server order; the server combines them in the opposite order.

Each side sends the other a message authentication code over its own view of the channel-binding data. This type applies only to TELNET, although it can be used with any TLS connection carrying TELNET.
sections.plainLanguage: The TELNET-specific type combines the two Finished values in opposite orders at the two endpoints. Each endpoint sends a message authentication code so the other can compare its view of the connection.

sections.title: Choosing a Binding Type
sections.content:
tls-unique works with all TLS connections. tls-server-end-point needs a server certificate, but can work through existing server-side TLS proxies without changing them. The RFC RECOMMENDS that application protocols use tls-unique, except that they MAY prefer the certificate-based type where proxies are common.

Security frameworks generally do not negotiate a binding type for their applications. Peers therefore need to agree beforehand. An application protocol MUST identify at least one type that implementations are required to support.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers need to agree on a binding type because their security framework may not choose one for them. The RFC prefers tls-unique, while noting that the certificate-based type can work better with some server-side proxies.

sections.title: APIs and Security Considerations
sections.content:
TLS implementations that support tls-unique or tls-unique-for-telnet MUST provide client and server applications with an API to obtain the connection's binding data. The RFC does not prescribe the API design. Implementations supporting renegotiation SHOULD let applications control when it occurs.

The channel-binding data does not have to remain secret. TLS Finished values are tied cryptographically to the connection, and a server certificate is also tied to the connection when present. The RFC warns that applications using TLS without secure renegotiation must follow additional safeguards before authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS software must let applications obtain supported channel-binding data. The data is not itself secret; its purpose is to show that both endpoints refer to the same protected connection.
